title: Buildings, Beauty, and the Brain: A Neuroscience of Architectural Experience
central_proposition: The nascent field of neuroarchitecture is at a pivotal point, poised to extend from applying neuroscientific knowledge to architecture to directly investigating architectural experiences using neuroscientific inquiry, guided by a general theoretical framework like the aesthetic triad.

concept_definitions.name: Neuroarchitecture
concept_definitions.definition: A burgeoning interdisciplinary field investigating the intersection of neuroscience and architecture, aiming to offer biologically inspired insights into the design of spaces that contribute to human flourishing.

concept_definitions.name: Aesthetic Triad
concept_definitions.definition: A general neural model proposing that aesthetic experiences are generated by three large-scale systems: sensorimotor, knowledge-meaning, and emotion-valuation.

concept_definitions.name: Firmitas
concept_definitions.definition: One of Vitruvius's three core dimensions of architectural design, referring to a building being strong and structurally stable.

concept_definitions.name: Utilitas
concept_definitions.definition: One of Vitruvius's three core dimensions of architectural design, referring to a building meeting the functional needs of its occupants.

concept_definitions.name: Venustas
concept_definitions.definition: One of Vitruvius's three core dimensions of architectural design, referring to a building appealing to aesthetic sensibilities.

concept_definitions.name: Processing Fluency
concept_definitions.definition: The ease with which visual configurations are processed, hypothesized to correlate with aesthetic preference.

concept_definitions.name: Habitat Theory
concept_definitions.definition: An evolutionary framework explaining psychological responses to architectural spaces, proposing that humans prefer landscapes/spaces containing visual features and spatial configurations that favor survival.

concept_definitions.name: Biophilia Hypothesis
concept_definitions.definition: The proposition that human sensory systems developed heightened sensitivity to living and life-like stimuli of the natural world.

concept_definitions.name: Prospect-Refuge
concept_definitions.definition: A concept within habitat theory suggesting visual preferences for environments that offer both clear views (prospect) and safe places to hide (refuge).

concept_definitions.name: Soft Fascinations
concept_definitions.definition: Inherently fascinating visual stimuli in natural landscapes (e.g., vegetation, wildlife, motion of leaves) that capture attention in a bottom-up fashion, allowing for attention restoration.

argument_structure: The paper establishes the historical importance of architectural aesthetics (Vitruvian triad) and its modern de-emphasis, then highlights a resurgence of interest in neuroarchitecture. It argues for the field's maturation into an experimental science, proposing the 'aesthetic triad' as a guiding theoretical framework. The authors elaborate on each component of the triad (sensorimotor, knowledge-meaning, emotion-valuation) with existing empirical evidence, discuss implications for health and well-being, and outline key challenges for future research.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Architectural experiences are proposed to arise from the interaction of three large-scale neural systems: 1) Sensorimotor systems process environmental features (visual, auditory, somatosensory, olfactory, vestibular), leading to basic perceptual processing (e.g., contrast, grouping, symmetry, fractal dimensions) and triggering motor responses (approach/avoidance, navigation). Processing fluency within these systems contributes to aesthetic preference. 2) Knowledge-meaning systems, informed by personal experiences, cultural background, education, and expectations (e.g., expertise, familiarity, context, intended function), shape how individuals interpret and evaluate built environments, influencing aesthetic judgments and emotional responses. 3) Emotion-valuation systems mediate feelings and emotions evoked by architectural features through brain reward circuitry (e.g., OFC, BG, ACC, insula) and stress response systems (e.g., amygdala, HPA axis). These emotional responses can be rapid, automatic, and evolutionarily adaptive, influencing behavior and long-term health. Conscious aesthetic judgments also involve prefrontal and memory systems. These systems interact, with sensory inputs providing raw data, knowledge systems framing its interpretation, and emotion systems assigning valence, all contributing to the emergent aesthetic experience.

findings.consequent: Peoples' flourishing in behavior, health, and well-being
findings.mechanism: Biologically inspired insights from neuroscience can motivate construction of environments that positively impact human experience.
findings.quote: The goal of such interdisciplinary approaches to architecture is to motivate construction of environments that would contribute to peoples' flourishing in behavior, health, and well-being.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies indicate aesthetic qualities impact mood, cognitive functioning, behavior, mental health (Adams, 2014; Cooper, Burton, & Cooper, 2014; Hartig, 2008; Joye, 2007).

findings.mechanism: The field of neuroarchitecture is moving beyond inferences from neuroscience applied to architecture, towards direct experimental work on architectural experience itself.
findings.quote: architectural experiences themselves are the target of neuroscientific inquiry.

findings.mechanism: These three large-scale systems interact to produce the emergent aesthetic experiences of architecture.
findings.quote: According to this model, three large-scale systems generate aesthetic experiences: sensorimotor, knowledge-meaning, and emotion-valuation systems
findings.empirical_support_cited: Originally created to frame aesthetic experiences in neural terms (Chatterjee, 2013; Shimamura, 2013).

findings.antecedent: Environmental features (visual, auditory, somatosensory, olfactory, vestibular systems)
findings.mechanism: Sensory networks act as 'gatekeepers' of architectural experience, processing environmental features.
findings.quote: Environmental features differentially stimulate our visual, auditory, somatosensory, vestibular, and olfactory neural networks.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Burke (1767) remarked on beauty acting mechanically upon the human mind by intervention of the senses.

findings.mechanism: Sensory inputs are tied to downstream motor responses, guiding interaction with the built environment.
findings.quote: These sensations are tied to downstream motor responses such as the affordances of objects, approach and avoidance reactions, and navigation through built spaces.

findings.antecedent: Basic low-level visual attributes (luminance, color, motion) and intermediate levels (grouping)
findings.consequent: Higher-level processing areas (parahippocampal place area, retrosplenial cortex, occipital place area)
findings.mechanism: Visual information undergoes hierarchical processing from basic features to complex scene representation.
findings.quote: Basic low-level visual attributes such as luminance, color, and motion and intermediate levels like grouping are processed (Chatterjee, 2004a) before integration into higher-level processing areas

findings.antecedent: Environmental scenes (landscapes, building interiors, urban neighborhoods)
findings.mechanism: The PPA is specialized for processing environmental scenes and plays a critical role in spatial navigation.
findings.quote: The parahippocampal place area responds specifically to environmental scenes, including landscapes, building interiors, and urban neighborhoods, and also plays a critical role in spatial navigation

findings.mechanism: The PPA's role in spatial representation extends to encoding the perceived size or openness of spaces.
findings.quote: This area also codes for the expansiveness of spaces (Kravitz, Peng, & Baker, 2011).

findings.antecedent: Perceptual features (building materials, windows, architectural motifs)
findings.mechanism: The OPA contributes to recognizing the interior and exterior of buildings by processing specific visual features.
findings.quote: Recent work suggests that the occipital place area is involved in processing perceptual features like building materials, windows, and architectural motifs that might be relevant to recognizing the interior and exterior of buildings.

findings.direction: retrieves information that allows people to orient themselves within
findings.mechanism: The RSC plays a role in spatial memory and orientation within familiar or imagined spaces.
findings.quote: By contrast, the retrosplenial cortex retrieves information that allows people to orient themselves within a remembered or imagined spatial environment (Marchette et al., 2015).

findings.direction: contributes to different aspects of spatial navigation relevant for
findings.mechanism: These regions are fundamental for spatial navigation and memory, which are crucial for interacting with built environments.
findings.quote: Hippocampal and entorhinal cortices contribute to different aspects of spatial navigation, which would be relevant for architectural experiences (Spiers & Barry, 2015).

findings.antecedent: Visual configurations with some degree of complexity that are also processed easily or fluently
findings.mechanism: Processing fluency, the ease with which the visual system processes information, mediates aesthetic preference.
findings.quote: humans prefer configurations with some degree of complexity that are also processed easily or fluently.

findings.mechanism: The visual system is tuned to these fundamental features, which are important for object identification and scene organization.
findings.quote: The visual system is sensitive to features like contrast, grouping, and symmetry (Ramachandran & Hirstein, 1999).

findings.mechanism: These regions contain a high density of useful visual information for object identification, drawing attention.
findings.quote: High-contrast regions often capture visual attention and interest because they contain a high density of useful visual information for object identification
findings.empirical_support_cited: Geisler, 2007; Brady & Field, 2000; Ramachandran & Hirstein, 1999; Hagerhall, Purcell, & Taylor, 2004; Leder et al., 2004; Alexander, 2002.

findings.antecedent: Grouped features (e.g., of color or form) in a scene
findings.consequent: Synchronized action potentials among associated neurons
findings.mechanism: Grouping, a Gestalt principle, describes how the visual system orders correlated information, leading to synchronized neural activity and mediating pleasure.
findings.quote: Grouped features (e.g., of color or form) trigger synchronized action potentials among associated neurons responsible for processing those features (Ramachandran & Hirstein, 1999; Singer & Gray, 1995).

findings.mechanism: Symmetry, as a straightforward example of balance, is an evolutionarily important fitness indicator, enabling efficient recognition and contributing to aesthetic appeal.
findings.quote: Balance, of which symmetry is the most straightforward example, also contributes to fluency and aesthetic preference (Wilson & Chatterjee, 2005).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Wilson & Chatterjee, 2005; Jacobsen et al., 2006; Ramachandran & Hirstein, 1999; Rhodes et al., 1998; Frith & Nias, 1974; Alexander & Carey, 1968.

findings.antecedent: Fractal dimensions (ranging from 1.3 to 1.5) in natural scenes, visual art, and computer-generated patterns
findings.mechanism: The visual system is sensitive to statistical properties of images, and fractal geometry provides a mathematical description of complex shapes found in nature, influencing aesthetic responses.
findings.quote: Aesthetic preferences for natural scenes, visual art, and computer-generated patterns seem to correlate moderately with fractal dimensions ranging from about 1.3 to 1.5
findings.empirical_support_cited: Taylor et al., 2005; Spehar et al., 2003; Hagerhall et al., 2004.

findings.antecedent: Moderate level of visual complexity in art and architectural interiors
findings.mechanism: Preferences tend to follow an inverted U-shaped curve in relation to complexity, where moderate levels are optimal for information processing without being overwhelming.
findings.quote: people generally prefer at least a moderate level of visual complexity when viewing both art and architectural interiors (Dosen & Ostwald, 2016; Leder et al., 2004; Frith & Nias, 1974).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Dosen & Ostwald, 2016; Leder et al., 2004; Frith & Nias, 1974; Berlyne, 1970, 1971; Güçlütürk, Jacobs, & van Lier, 2016; Imamoglu, 2000.

findings.mechanism: Too much information or disorganized information can exceed the processing capacity of the visual system, leading to negative experiences.
findings.quote: Excess architectural complexity may also overwhelm the visual system, particularly if the information is experienced as disorganized (Kotabe et al., 2016; Salingaros, 2003, 2007).

findings.antecedent: Landscapes/spaces containing visual features and spatial configurations that favor survival (e.g., prospect-refuge)
findings.mechanism: According to habitat theory, humans evolved to prefer environments that signal safety and nourishment, which were crucial for early hominid survival.
findings.quote: Appleton's habitat theory offers an evolutionary framework to explain psychological responses to architectural spaces. According to habitat theory, humans evolved to prefer landscapes containing visual features and spatial configurations that favor survival (Appleton, 1975).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Appleton, 1975; Joye, 2007; Balling & Falk, 1982; Dosen & Ostwald, 2016.

findings.mechanism: Openness may be interpreted as greater visual prospect, which is preferred due to evolutionary predispositions for survival.
findings.quote: In an fMRI study of architectural interiors, we found that participants judged open rooms as more beautiful than enclosed rooms (Vartanian et al., 2015).

findings.consequent: Left middle temporal gyrus and right superior temporal gyrus activity (associated with perceived visual motion)
findings.mechanism: The visual experience of open spaces may involve perceived motion, contributing to their aesthetic appeal.
findings.quote: Open interiors activated structures in the temporal lobes associated with perceived visual motion, including the left middle temporal gyrus and the right superior temporal gyrus (Vartanian et al., 2015).

findings.mechanism: Higher ceilings may be interpreted as providing greater visual prospect, aligning with evolutionary preferences for expansive views.
findings.quote: Participants in this study also preferred rooms with higher ceilings over those with lower ceilings, which could be interpreted as a preference for greater visual prospect.

findings.consequent: Visuo-spatial attention and exploration areas (left precuneus, left middle frontal gyrus) activity
findings.mechanism: Greater visual prospect afforded by high ceilings engages neural systems involved in spatial attention and exploration.
findings.quote: high ceilings activated structures associated with visuo-spatial attention and exploration, including the left precuneus and the left middle frontal gyrus (Vartanian et al., 2015).

findings.antecedent: Living and life-like stimuli of the natural world
findings.mechanism: E.O. Wilson's biophilia hypothesis proposes an innate human affiliation with nature, leading to heightened sensory responses to natural elements.
findings.quote: E.O. Wilson's biophilia hypothesis proposes that our sensory systems developed heightened sensitivity to living and life-like stimuli of the natural world (Wilson, 1984).

findings.antecedent: Inherently fascinating visual stimuli in natural landscapes (vegetation, wildlife, motion of leaves)
findings.mechanism: These 'soft fascinations' capture attention in a bottom-up fashion, allowing for cognitive restoration.
findings.quote: Kaplan and colleagues proposed that inherently fascinating visual stimuli in natural landscapes, like vegetation, wildlife, and “the motion of leaves in the breeze" (Kaplan, 1995, p. 174), capture the attention of our visual system in a bottom-up fashion
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kaplan, 1995; Berman et al., 2014; Berman, Jonides, & Kaplan, 2008; Ulrich & Parsons, 1992.

findings.antecedent: Biomorphic features in human construction (ornamentation, scaling, proportionality, structural support schemes inspired by plants and animals)
findings.mechanism: Drawing inspiration from nature in architectural design may tap into innate biophilic preferences, leading to positive sensory and emotional responses.
findings.quote: Several authors have speculated about the potential sensory and emotional benefits of naturalistic patterns in architecture, like curvilinear form and fractal scaling (Joye, 2007; Salingaros, 2007; Alexander, 2002).

findings.consequent: Lingual and calcarine gyrus activity in visual cortex
findings.direction: activates more than rectilinear interiors when making approach-avoidance choices
findings.mechanism: Curvilinear forms may engage specific visual processing areas differently, potentially influencing approach-avoidance behaviors.
findings.quote: we, for instance, found that images of curvilinear architectural interiors activated the lingual and the calcarine gyrus in the visual cortex more than images of rectilinear interiors when participants made approach-avoidance choices (Vartanian et al., 2013).

findings.consequent: Occupant's emotional response to a building
findings.mechanism: There is a direct link between the olfactory system and the limbic system, which processes emotions.
findings.quote: Odor affects an occupant's emotional response to a building (Barbara & Perliss, 2006), perhaps because of the direct link between the olfactory and limbic system (Ward, 2015).

findings.consequent: Memories of past experiences in a place (e.g., childhood home)
findings.mechanism: Olfaction activates neural structures governing memory, affect, and meaning, linking smells to specific past contexts.
findings.quote: Olfaction can revive memories of past experiences in a place, like a childhood home, by activating neural structures governing memory, affect, and meaning (Lehrer, 2008).

findings.consequent: Fullness and complexity of sound perceived, and whether a place is designed for contemplation or excitement
findings.mechanism: Audition provides information about the size and shape of architectural space, and acoustic qualities influence the emotional and cognitive experience of the space.
findings.quote: Acoustic parameters like reverberation time affect the fullness and complexity of the sound perceived and probably contributes to whether a place is designed for contemplation as in a monastery or for excitement as in a stadium.

findings.antecedent: Occupant's tactile and thermal sensations of buildings
findings.mechanism: The somatosensory cortex processes bodily sensations, including touch and temperature, from the environment.
findings.quote: The somatosensory cortex mediates an occupant's tactile and thermal sensations of buildings.

findings.consequent: Occupant's comfort, emotional state, and perception of beauty
findings.mechanism: Thermal sensations are integrated with affective and evaluative processes, impacting overall experience.
findings.quote: A building's temperature, for instance, influences an occupant's comfort, emotional state, and perception of beauty
findings.empirical_support_cited: Thorsson et al., 2007; Nicol & Humphreys, 2002; Fanger, 1973.

findings.consequent: Neural areas responsible for motor planning and navigation
findings.mechanism: The design of spaces influences how people plan and execute movement, engaging specific neural circuits for navigation.
findings.quote: Navigating buildings involves planning and execution of movement, and it is likely that architectural design differentially impacts neural areas responsible for motor planning and navigation.

findings.mechanism: The global pallidus is involved in motor responses, suggesting a link between aesthetic judgment and potential motor actions or readiness.
findings.quote: Beauty evaluations of architecture can vary with neural activity in the global pallidus (Vartanian et al., 2013), perhaps suggestive of motor responses (Nambu, Tokuno, & Takada, 2002).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Vartanian et al., 2013; Nambu, Tokuno, & Takada, 2002.

findings.consequent: Decisions to approach or avoid a space
findings.mechanism: These decisions are governed by reward and emotion processing areas, linking aesthetic features to motivational behaviors.
findings.quote: Aesthetic parameters like enclosure has an impact on decisions to approach or avoid a space (Vartanian et al., 2015), which may be governed by reward and emotion processing areas like the nucleus accumbens, the anterior insula, and the basolateral amygdala (Vartanian et al., 2013).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Vartanian et al., 2015; Vartanian et al., 2013.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to images of tall buildings (associated with heightened feelings of awe)
findings.consequent: Greater immobility and slower manual clicking task response
findings.mechanism: Awe-evoking monumental buildings can trigger a behavioral freezing response, influencing motor activity and the quality of experience.
findings.quote: Joye and Dewitte found that exposure to images of tall buildings—which were associated with heightened feelings of awe—caused participants to experience greater immobility and to respond more slowly on a manual clicking task than exposure to images of low buildings (Joye & Dewitte, 2016).

findings.antecedent: Education, memories, and context in which a person encounters an aesthetic object or built environment
findings.mechanism: These factors shape the interpretation and evaluation of aesthetic stimuli, influencing cognitive and affective responses.
findings.quote: Education, memories, and the context in which a person encounters an aesthetic object or a built environment can have an impact on the person's experience.

findings.consequent: Increased activation of reward circuitry (bilateral medial OFC, subcallosal cingulate gyrus) when making aesthetic judgments about buildings
findings.mechanism: Expertise modulates neural responses to aesthetic stimuli, potentially by enhancing reward processing for domain-specific objects.
findings.quote: Another experiment showed that architects, compared with nonarchitects, had increased activation of reward circuitry, including the bilateral medial OFC and the subcallosal cingulate gyrus, when making aesthetic judgments about buildings (Kirk, Skov, Christensen, & Nygaard, 2009).

findings.antecedent: Architects (compared with control participants) viewing buildings (but not faces)
findings.consequent: Greater activation of hippocampus and precuneus
findings.mechanism: Memories from education and professional experience contribute to architects' affective responses to buildings, engaging memory retrieval systems.
findings.quote: Architects also exhibited greater activation of the hippocampus and precuneus compared with control participants when viewing buildings but not faces, suggesting that memories rendered by education and professional experience contributed to their affective responses.

findings.consequent: Cognitive map using place and grid cells of the hippocampus
findings.mechanism: The hippocampus forms a cognitive map of space, which facilitates efficient navigation in future encounters.
findings.quote: Exposure to an environment generates a cognitive map using place and grid cells of the hippocampus (McNaughton, Battaglia, Jensen, Moser, & Moser, 2006; O'keefe & Nadel, 1978), which in turn facilitates more efficient navigation in future encounters
findings.empirical_support_cited: McNaughton et al., 2006; O'keefe & Nadel, 1978; Astur et al., 2002; Maguire et al., 2000.

findings.antecedent: Familiarity and ease of navigation in spaces
findings.mechanism: Familiarity influences liking, and efficient navigation reduces cognitive load, contributing to a more positive aesthetic experience.
findings.quote: Because familiarity influences liking (Montoya, Horton, Vevea, Citkowicz, & Lauber, 2017), we suspect that familiarity and ease of navigation would influence the aesthetic experience of spaces.

findings.antecedent: Occupants who control environmental parameters (building temperature, operable windows, fans, thermostats)
findings.consequent: Tolerance for a wider range of indoor temperatures
findings.mechanism: The perception of control over one's environment influences thermal comfort and physiological regulation.
findings.quote: Occupants who control environmental parameters affecting building temperature, such as operable windows, fans, and thermostats, tolerate a wider range of indoor temperatures than inhabitants with restricted control over their indoor climate (Nicol & Humphreys, 2002).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Nicol & Humphreys, 2002; Brager et al., 2004; Bauman et al., 1994.

findings.antecedent: Abstract visual art labeled as 'gallery pieces' (compared to 'computer-generated images')
findings.mechanism: Participants' expectations about aesthetic value, influenced by context and cultural meaning, shape their emotional responses and judgments.
findings.quote: Kirk and colleagues found that participants were more likely to judge abstract visual art as beautiful if they were labeled as gallery pieces than if they were classified as computer-generated images (Kirk, Skov, Hulme, Christensen, & Zeki, 2009).

findings.consequent: Increased activity in prefrontal, orbitofrontal, and entorhinal cortices
findings.mechanism: Expectations about aesthetic value, influenced by semantic context, modulate neural activity in regions associated with valuation and memory.
findings.quote: Art randomly assigned the "gallery" label generated increased activity in prefrontal, orbitofrontal, and entorhinal cortices than those assigned the “computer” label, indicating that participants' expectations about the aesthetic value of the artworks influenced their emotional responses.

findings.antecedent: Building's advertised cultural significance, design by famous architects, perceived sustainability, historical period, or intended function
findings.mechanism: Knowledge and context provide a frame of mind that biases perception and evaluation, influencing how a building is experienced.
findings.quote: Similar to the gallery condition for art, a building's advertised cultural significance could shape an occupant's expectations and alter his or her experience of the space.

findings.consequent: Core neural circuit involving OFC, BG, ACC, and anterior insula activity
findings.mechanism: The brain's reward circuitry mediates the emotions felt in the presence of beautiful architecture.
findings.quote: Brown and colleagues proposed that the processing of aesthetic emotions occurs through a core neural circuit involving the OFC, the BG, the ACC, and the anterior insula (Brown, Gao, Tisdelle, Eickhoff, & Liotti, 2011).

findings.antecedent: Curvilinear building interiors (compared to rectilinear spaces)
findings.mechanism: Curvilinear forms may be inherently more appealing, engaging specific neural circuits associated with positive affect.
findings.quote: Our study revealed that curvilinear building interiors are judged as more beautiful and pleasing than rectilinear spaces and that beauty ratings of curved rooms correlated with increased activation of ACC (Vartanian et al., 2013).

findings.mechanism: The ACC is involved in reward processing and coactivated with OFC and anterior insula, indicating its role in positive aesthetic valuation.
findings.quote: beauty ratings of curved rooms correlated with increased activation of ACC (Vartanian et al., 2013). ACC is connected with both the OFC and anterior insula and is often coactivated with these regions in neuroimaging studies rewards (Brown et al., 2011).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Vartanian et al., 2013; Brown et al., 2011.

findings.mechanism: Enclosed spaces may trigger negative emotional responses, mediated by brain regions involved in fear processing.
findings.quote: A follow-up experiment found that participants' inclinations to exit enclosed rooms, compared with open rooms, were associated with activation of the anterior midcingulate cortex (Vartanian et al., 2015).

findings.mechanism: The anterior midcingulate cortex receives projections from the amygdala and is involved in fear processing, linking enclosed spaces to negative emotional states.
findings.quote: The anterior midcingulate cortex receives direct projections from the amygdala (Vogt & Pandya, 1987) and is involved in fear processing (Whalen et al., 1998), pointing out that brain circuitry governing negative emotions almost certainly play a role in architectural experience.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Vartanian et al., 2015; Vogt & Pandya, 1987; Whalen et al., 1998.

findings.antecedent: Immersion in a virtual simulation of an enclosed room without windows (compared to a virtual room with windows)
findings.consequent: Greater reactivity to a stress test (heightened and prolonged spikes in salivary cortisol)
findings.mechanism: Enclosed environments without natural views can induce physiological stress responses, mediated by limbic structures like the amygdala modulating neuroendocrine and autonomic nervous systems.
findings.quote: study participants immersed in a virtual simulation of an enclosed room without windows exhibited greater reactivity to a stress test than participants who undertook the test in a virtual room with windows (Fich et al., 2014).

findings.antecedent: Chronic exposure to maladaptive built environments
findings.mechanism: The close association between the limbic system and stress responses suggests a pathway by which chronic stress from poor environments affects health.
findings.quote: The close association between the limbic system and stress responses represents a key pathway by which chronic exposure to maladaptive built environments might negatively impact an occupant's long-term health (Joye, 2007).

findings.direction: are primarily influenced by automatic, unconscious processing
findings.mechanism: Ulrich's framework suggests that the visual and limbic systems work in concert to rapidly identify and evaluate incoming visual information.
findings.quote: The idea that the visual and limbic systems work in concert to rapidly identify and evaluate incoming visual information is consistent with Ulrich's framework, which proposes that initial affective responses toward environments are primarily influenced by automatic, unconscious processing (Ulrich, 1983).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Ulrich, 1983; Joye & Dewitte, 2016; Valtchanov & Ellard, 2015; Hietanen & Korpela, 2004; Korpela, Klemettilä, & Hietanen, 2002.

findings.mechanism: Rapid emotional responses are adaptive by relieving people of the cost imposed by learning an environment through actual lived experience.
findings.quote: Such a quick emotional response could be adaptive by relieving people of the cost imposed by learning an environment through actual lived experience (Joye, 2007; Kaplan, 1987; Ulrich, 1983).

findings.antecedent: Evolutionary basis for aesthetic sensation and emotion
findings.consequent: Architects manipulating design parameters of buildings
findings.mechanism: If aesthetics have an evolutionary basis, design elements like contrast, grouping, and symmetry, which appear ubiquitously in vernacular architecture, could be intentionally used to evoke positive responses.
findings.quote: If there is indeed an evolutionary basis for aesthetic sensation and emotion, then architects could manipulate the design parameters of their buildings to heighten these adaptive responses.

findings.consequent: Activity in pFC (frontopolar cortex, superior frontal gyrus) and memory retrieval regions (parahippocampus)
findings.mechanism: Aesthetic judgment involves conscious reasoning, analysis, and memory processes, distinct from reward circuitry.
findings.quote: In one study, beauty judgments of architecture were shown to vary with activity in various regions of the pFC, including the frontopolar cortex and the superior frontal gyrus, as well as brain regions involved in memory retrieval, such as the parahippocampus (Vartanian et al., 2013).

findings.consequent: Inputs from knowledge-meaning systems (expertise, cultural trends, understanding of building's intended function)
findings.mechanism: Conscious aesthetic judgment integrates cognitive and contextual information, suggesting a top-down influence on valuation.
findings.quote: Increased activity in both of these neural regions implies that aesthetic judgment may be particularly influenced by inputs from the knowledge-meaning systems such as expertise, cultural trends, and an understanding of a building's intended function.

findings.antecedent: Aesthetic judgment tasks (compared to passive observation)
findings.consequent: Emotional responses to visual art (e.g., insula activation)
findings.mechanism: Explicit evaluation may engage cognitive control that suppresses or modulates automatic emotional processing.
findings.quote: Do Dio and colleagues found that aesthetic judgment tasks actually diminish emotional responses to visual art. Participants who were asked to rate the beauty of Renaissance sculptures showed decreased activation in the right insula compared with those who were merely instructed to passively observe the sculptures (Di Dio, Macaluso, & Rizzolatti, 2007).

findings.consequent: Blood pressure and adolescent neural development
findings.mechanism: Environmental stressors like noise can have direct physiological and developmental impacts.
findings.quote: chronic exposure to unwanted noise can increase blood pressure (Payne, Potter, & Cain, 2014) and hinder adolescent neural development (Gilbert & Galea, 2014).

findings.mechanism: Light exposure is critical for regulating the body's internal clock and sleep-wake cycles.
findings.quote: Insufficient daylight may affect circadian rhythms and impair sleep quality (Dutton, 2014).

findings.mechanism: Color can modulate cognitive processing styles, with red potentially enhancing focus on details.
findings.quote: immersion in red environments may improve performance on detail-oriented cognitive tasks

findings.mechanism: Color can modulate cognitive processing styles, with blue potentially enhancing creativity.
findings.quote: blue spaces might be associated with enhanced creative thinking (Mehta & Zhu, 2009).

findings.antecedent: Greenery and other natural features in the built environment
findings.consequent: Mood, working memory, stress recovery, and surgery recovery
findings.mechanism: Natural elements provide restorative benefits, reducing physiological stress and cognitive fatigue.
findings.quote: greenery and other natural features in the built environment may improve mood (Bowler, Buyung-Ali, Knight, & Pullin, 2010), enhance working memory (Bratman, Daily, Levy, & Gross, 2015), and accelerate recovery from stress (Ulrich et al., 1991) and surgery (Ulrich, 1984).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Bowler et al., 2010; Bratman et al., 2015; Ulrich et al., 1991; Ulrich, 1984.

findings.consequent: Likelihood of patients with Alzheimer's disease getting lost
findings.mechanism: Lack of distinct visual reference points hinders spatial orientation and navigation for individuals with cognitive impairments.
findings.quote: Monotonous interior architectural composition can make patients with Alzheimer's disease more likely to get lost

findings.antecedent: Incorporating frequent visual reference points and exterior views in interior architectural composition
findings.consequent: Navigation for patients with Alzheimer's disease
findings.mechanism: Clear visual cues and connections to the outside environment aid spatial orientation and reduce disorientation.
findings.quote: whereas incorporating frequent visual reference points and exterior views can improve their navigation (Passini, Pigot, Rainville, & Tétreault, 2000).

findings.mechanism: Design characteristics that improve physical and mental health are linked to the perceived attractiveness of the environment.
findings.quote: Increasing evidence from these investigations suggests that "attractiveness is a key element in how the built environment affects our wellbeing" (Cooper & Burton, 2014, p. 13).

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: How aesthetic experiences mediate the effects of architecture on behavior, health, and well-being.
How differences in building types (e.g., homes, hospitals, office space, museums) might modulate the nature of aesthetic experiences.
Understanding the similarities and differences in people's responses to built versus natural environments.
Investigating the neural underpinnings of complex emotional responses to architecture like contemplation, comfort, curiosity, and awe.
Understanding potential interactions between aesthetic emotion and evaluation.
How to incorporate different modalities and probe the neural underpinnings of an integrated sensory-motor experience.
How to sample neurophysiological data over prolonged time and 'in the field'.
Developing ecologically valid approaches to measure deep psychological states (contemplation, social cohesion, refuge, alienation) in response to built spaces.
bridge_warrants: The paper applies the 'aesthetic triad' model, originally developed for neuroaesthetics, to the domain of architectural experience, thereby bridging these two fields.

It integrates concepts from environmental psychology, such as Habitat Theory, Biophilia Hypothesis, Prospect-Refuge Theory, Attention Restoration Theory, and Stress Recovery Theory, with neuroscientific mechanisms to explain architectural experience.
The framework incorporates Gestalt principles (e.g., grouping, symmetry) and concepts of processing fluency from cognitive psychology into a neuroscientific model of aesthetic preference.
It acknowledges and seeks to integrate dual-process models of cognition (automatic vs. conscious processing) into the understanding of aesthetic responses to architecture.
methodological_critiques: Current neuroarchitecture research is predominantly descriptive and lacks a general theoretical framework for programmatic investigation.
Most neuroaesthetics and neuroarchitecture research relies on 2-D images, which do not capture the immersive and multisensory nature of real architectural experiences.
There is a challenge in experimentally capturing the specific, prolonged, and habitual experience of being in a real architectural space.
The field faces challenges in incorporating different sensory modalities and probing the neural underpinnings of an integrated multisensory-motor experience.
There is a need for methods to sample neurophysiological data over prolonged durations and 'in the field' to capture the temporal dynamics of architectural engagement.

The field needs to expand its scope beyond the study of simple preferences to include a focus on deeper psychological states (e.g., contemplation, social cohesion, refuge, alienation) and develop ecologically valid measurement approaches.
model_structure: The paper proposes the 'aesthetic triad' as a general neural model for architectural experience. This model posits that aesthetic experiences are generated by the interaction of three large-scale systems: 1) Sensorimotor systems (processing visual, auditory, somatosensory, olfactory, and vestibular inputs and triggering motor responses), 2) Knowledge-meaning systems (incorporating personal experiences, culture, and education), and 3) Emotion-valuation networks (mediating feelings and emotions). These systems are depicted as interconnected components contributing to the overall aesthetic experience.
limitations: The nascent field of neuroarchitecture currently lacks a general theoretical framework to guide programmatic research, leading to isolated findings.
Existing neuroaesthetics research, often using 2-D images, does not adequately capture the immersive and multisensory nature of real architectural experiences.

There are significant measurement challenges related to the dimensionality, multimodality, temporality (prolonged engagement), and depth of psychological processing involved in architectural experiences.

The 'double framing' problem highlights the need for both general theoretical frameworks (like the aesthetic triad) and specific contextual frames (e.g., building function, user expectations) to guide research effectively.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: An isovist, or viewshed, is the area in a spatial environment directly visible from a location within the space. Here we show how a set of isovists can be used to generate a graph of mutual visibility between locations. We demonstrate that this graph can also be constructed without reference to isovists and that we are in fact invoking the more general concept of a visibility graph. Using the visibility graph, we can extend both isovist and current graph-based analyses of architectural space to form a new methodology for the investigation of configurational relationships. The measurement of local and global characteristics of the graph, for each vertex or for the system as a whole, is of interest from an architectural perspective, allowing us to describe a configuration with reference to accessibility and visibility, to compare from location to location within a system, and to compare systems with different geometries. Finally we show that visibility graph properties may be closely related to manifestations of spatial perception, such as way-finding, movement, and space use.
